chapter_title: Data Types and Variables in Solidity

screens.title: Data Types and Variables in Solidity
screens.subtitle: How values are stored, copied, and accessed — choosing the right type and location matters for correctness and gas.

narration.text: In this chapter you'll build a mental model of how Solidity stores and moves data. We'll start by drawing a clear line between value types, which contain the data itself, and reference types, which contain pointers to where data lives. You'll see common examples — booleans, unsigned integers, addresses, fixed bytes, arrays, structs, and mappings — and learn the practical rule: pick the smallest, safest type that expresses your intent. We'll also step through data locations: storage is persistent and expensive, memory is temporary and cheaper. That distinction explains a lot of tricky bugs and gas surprises you may meet in smart contract work. For each type we'll ground the idea with short code examples and a small safety checklist: when to use address payable, why integer sizing saves gas, and how returning an array requires an in-memory copy. By the end you should be able to choose types to reduce gas, avoid accidental state writes, and express contract invariants more safely. Think of this as the foundation for robust contracts — small type choices ripple into correctness and cost. What is one type choice you already make instinctively, and why?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Value types store data directly and copy on assignment; reference types point to storage and can share underlying data. Storage vs. memory decides persistence and gas cost.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Data Types & Variables
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Data Types & Variables

Understand what you store, where you store it, and how assignments behave.

16:9 HD Classroom
Value Types

Store data directly. Copy on assignment. Examples: uint, bool, address.

Reference Types

Store pointers to data. Assignments copy references. Examples: arrays, structs, mappings.

Orientation

Why types and locations matter

Solidity is deployed to a shared ledger and every storage write costs gas. Choosing types carefully makes your contract safer and cheaper. Small types can reduce gas; wrong locations can cause accidental state modification.

Example
Use uint8 for age and address payable when you intend to send Ether.
Misconception
Reference assignment copies the pointer, not the data — changes can affect the original storage.
Visual Concept
Value box
Contains actual data. Copying creates independent value.
uint myNumber = 42;
Reference pointer
Contains a location pointer. Multiple refs can point to the same storage.
uint[] storage arr = myArray;
Explore Key Topics
Value Types
Booleans, integers, addresses — copy semantics and gas implications.
Reference Types
Arrays, strings, structs, and mappings — storage vs. memory matters.
Safety
Integer overflows, payable addresses, and avoiding accidental state writes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide your learning. First, you will clearly differentiate value types from reference types. That distinction informs how data copies behave and how state changes propagate. Second, you will identify and use the common value types: unsigned and signed integers, booleans, addresses, and fixed-size bytes. You'll learn practical uses, like using uint for balances and address payable for recipients. Third, you will understand fixed-size and dynamic arrays and when to store them in storage or memory. This affects gas and correctness. Fourth, you'll explain the difference between storage and memory in function contexts and choose the right data location to avoid accidental persistent writes. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can check that you apply the rules while coding. For example, when returning an array from a view function, you will know to return a memory copy. When deciding integer width, you'll weigh gas savings against safe ranges. These skills reduce bugs and gas costs and help you write clearer, safer contracts.

keyIdea.title: Objectives
keyIdea.text: Master the type categories, choose efficient sizes, and pick correct data locations to avoid costly or unsafe behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Focus
screens.subtitle: Translate objectives into code patterns and checks

narration.text: This second objectives slide frames the same learning goals as practical checks you can use while coding. First, when you see a variable that should never be negative, replace int with uint and choose the smallest width that covers the range — for example uint8 for ages. Second, when dealing with recipients or contracts, mark addresses as payable if you will transfer Ether. Third, for functions that return arrays, remember that public state arrays will be copied to memory for the caller; specify memory in the return signature. Fourth, keep temporary collections in memory when possible and avoid creating storage references inside functions unless you intentionally want to modify state. Each of these checks helps you reduce gas and avoid subtle bugs. Make these checks part of your code review checklist: data range, payable intent, return location, and storage side effects. Practicing these will make your contracts more predictable and less costly.

keyIdea.title: Practical checks
keyIdea.text: When coding, verify range, payable intent, return locations, and whether a temporary value should be memory or storage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Practical Objectives

Objectives — Code Checklist

Turn learning aims into habits while you write or review contracts.

Range check
Use the smallest uint that fits your domain. Example: uint8 for ages up to 120. Small widths reduce storage and can reduce gas cost when packed.
Payable intent
Declare address payable when you plan to send Ether. This prevents accidental transfers to non-payable addresses.
Return location
When returning arrays, return a memory copy. Solidity requires the return type to specify memory so callers receive a snapshot, not a storage pointer.
Storage side effects
Avoid assigning storage references for temporary edits. Use memory copies unless you intend to update persistent state.

screens.title: Value Types — definition and examples
screens.subtitle: What it means that a variable stores its value directly

narration.text: Value types are the simplest Solidity types: the variable holds the actual data, and copying that variable produces an independent duplicate. That means if you assign one value type variable to another and later change the second, the first remains unchanged. Common value types include booleans, signed and unsigned integers, addresses, fixed-size byte arrays, and enums. A concrete example: if you write uint balance = 100; and then uint copy = balance; changing copy to 50 does not alter balance. This behavior matters because it prevents accidental cross-variable mutations for primitive data and it simplifies reasoning about gas: copying a small value is cheap and safe. A common misconception is thinking that choosing narrower integer sizes always saves gas in every context; while packing can reduce storage slots, operations and ABI encoding sometimes default to 256-bit words. The practical rule is to select the smallest type that safely expresses your domain and to measure gas when optimizing. Key takeaway: use value types when you need independent data copies and clear, predictable behavior. Value Types — definition and examples means directly store data; assignments create independent copies. use for booleans, integers, addresses, bytesn, and enums.. In practical terms, what it means that a variable stores its value directly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Value types
keyIdea.text: Directly store data; assignments create independent copies. Use for booleans, integers, addresses, bytesN, and enums.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Value Types
Definition

Value Types store data directly

When you assign a value type variable, you copy the underlying value. Later changes do not affect the original.

Example
uint public tokenSupply = 1_000_000_000;
uint copy = tokenSupply; // copy is independent
Misconception
Using smaller integer types always reduces gas. Reality: slot packing helps storage, but computation and external interfaces may still use 256-bit words.
Key Takeaway

Choose value types for primitive data that should not share state. Copying produces independent values.

Common Value Types
Booleans
Used for flags and conditions. Example: bool public isActive = true;
Integers
Signed and unsigned with bit sizes from 8 to 256. Default is int256/uint256.
Address & bytesN
Address holds a 20-byte account; bytesN stores fixed raw bytes, e.g., bytes32 for hashes.
Concrete example
bool public isActive = true;
uint8 public age = 30;
bytes32 public documentHash;

screens.title: Integers and Booleans — sizing and safety
screens.subtitle: Choosing int, uint, and bit widths; overflow behavior and best practices

narration.text: Integers are fundamental in contracts: balances, counters, and identifiers use them. Solidity provides signed and unsigned integers across bit widths from 8 to 256. The shorthand uint and int map to 256-bit defaults. Practical guidance: use unsigned integers when negative values are illogical, like token balances, and choose the smallest width that safely covers your range. For example, age fits into uint8. Before Solidity 0.8.0, arithmetic could wrap around silently; now arithmetic overflow and underflow triggers a revert by default, improving safety. However, developers still need to be mindful if they use unchecked blocks for micro-optimizations. A concrete example from the chapter shows uint public tokenSupply = 1_000_000_000; and uint8 public age = 30;. A common pitfall is assuming a smaller width always reduces gas in every operation. While storage packing into single slots saves space, external calls and EVM operations often use 256-bit words. The best pattern is to reason about storage layout, test gas, and prefer clarity unless you measure a meaningful benefit from tighter packing. Question: which integer width would you pick for a counter that will not exceed one million?

keyIdea.title: Integer guidance
keyIdea.text: Prefer unsigned for non-negative data, pick widths that match domain, and trust Solidity 0.8+ automatic checks for overflow safety.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Integers & Booleans
Code Walkthrough

Sizing and examples

// Unsigned and signed examples
uint public tokenSupply = 1_000_000_000; // good for large positive counts
int public temperature = -5;             // signed for negative values
uint8 public age = 30;                   // compact storage for age
Solidity defaults to 256-bit, but you can pick smaller widths to pack storage. Confirm packing by checking how variables lay out in storage slots.
Safety notes
Overflow/Underflow
Since Solidity 0.8.0 arithmetic that exceeds limits will revert. If you use unchecked blocks you lose that protection and must manage wrap behavior carefully.
Concrete decision example
For a counter up to one million, uint32 or uint40 would suffice. Use the smallest type that fits and consider slot packing with adjacent variables.
Key Takeaway

Match integer types to domain constraints and avoid micro-optimizations without measuring gas impact.

screens.title: Address and address payable
screens.subtitle: Representing accounts and safely sending Ether

narration.text: Addresses are a dedicated value type for 20-byte Ethereum locations. They represent both externally owned accounts and contract accounts. The important practical split is address versus address payable. Use address payable when you intend to send Ether to that address; marking an address payable is a safety signal that prevents accidental transfers to non-payable addresses. In the constructor example provided in the chapter, contractOwner is assigned from a constructor parameter, and recipient is explicitly payable. This guards against accidentally trying to send Ether to an address that cannot accept it. Think of address as the identity and address payable as the identity plus a payment channel. A common misconception is that every address can receive Ether by default; the payable type enforces intent. When you design functions that transfer funds, require address payable parameters or cast explicitly with payable(someAddress) where appropriate. This habit reduces accidental reverts and clarifies your contract's transfer logic. Address and address payable means use address for identity; use address payable when you will transfer ether. this enforces intent and reduces accidental failures.. In practical terms, representing accounts and safely sending ether. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Address types
keyIdea.text: Use address for identity; use address payable when you will transfer Ether. This enforces intent and reduces accidental failures.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Address Types
Definition

address and address payable

Address holds a 20-byte account identifier. address payable signals that the address can receive Ether and is used where transfers will occur.

Code example
address public owner;
address payable public recipient;

constructor(address _owner, address payable _recipient) {
  owner = _owner;
  recipient = _recipient;
}
Why it matters
Using address payable clarifies intent and avoids accidental transfers. When executing send or transfer operations, the EVM requires a payable address to accept Ether. This prevents mistaken transfers that would otherwise revert or fail silently depending on context.
Misconception
Assuming all addresses accept Ether. Use payable typing to make the intent explicit and safe.
Key Takeaway

Declare payable addresses when you plan to send Ether; otherwise use plain address for identity-only roles.

screens.title: Fixed-size bytes and enums
screens.subtitle: Using bytesN for raw data and enums for constrained states

narration.text: Fixed-size byte arrays, from bytes1 to bytes32, are value types for raw binary data. They are efficient for storing hashes or compact identifiers; for example a document hash often fits in bytes32. Because they are fixed-size and value types, assignments copy the whole byte array value. Enums are user-defined value types that restrict a variable to a set of named constants, like Pending, Approved, and Rejected. Enums make code more readable and reduce invalid states by constraining possible values. In practice, use enums for finite state machines inside contracts and bytesN when you need a compact representation for fixed-length data. Watch out for using enums for extensible state: adding or reordering enum entries later changes the underlying numeric values and can break storage compatibility. The rule is to prefer fixed bytes for binary identifiers and enums for small, stable enumerations of states. This pairing helps clarity and gas efficiency when used intentionally. Fixed-size bytes and enums means bytesn stores fixed-length binary data; enums constrain values to named options. both are value types and copy on assignment.. In practical terms, using bytesn for raw data and enums for constrained states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bytes and Enums
keyIdea.text: bytesN stores fixed-length binary data; enums constrain values to named options. Both are value types and copy on assignment.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › bytesN & Enums
Fixed-size bytes

bytes1 ... bytes32

Use for fixed-length binary data such as hashes and IDs. They store raw bytes and are copied on assignment.

Example
bytes32 public documentHash; // ideal for cryptographic hashes
Enums

Constrained named states

Enums restrict values to a small, readable set and improve code clarity when representing finite states.

Example
enum State { Pending, Approved, Rejected }
State public currentState;

constructor() { currentState = State.Pending; }
Key Takeaway

Use bytesN for fixed binary values and enums for stable, finite states. Avoid reordering enum entries after deployment.

screens.title: Reference Types — arrays, strings, structs, mappings
screens.subtitle: Pointers, shared data, and where they live

narration.text: Reference types differ from value types because variables store pointers to data rather than the raw data itself. The common reference types include arrays, strings, structs, and mappings. When you assign a reference type variable you copy the pointer; both references then point to the same underlying data. This allows efficient sharing of large data structures but introduces potential side effects: modifying through one reference will be visible through others. Reference types also require explicit data location keywords inside functions — memory or storage — to make intent clear. For example, dynamic arrays declared as state variables live in storage, while arrays created inside a function should be declared memory unless you intend to reference storage. Strings are dynamic byte arrays for UTF-8 data and are reference types as well, so concatenation can be gas-intensive. Structs let you group multiple fields into a single type and are especially useful for modeling complex entities. Mappings act as storage hash tables and cannot be iterated, but they are efficient lookups for persistent state. The key pattern is: when you need persistence use storage, when you need a temporary copy use memory.

keyIdea.title: Reference types
keyIdea.text: Store pointers; assignments copy pointers not data. Choose storage for persistent state and memory for temporary processing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Reference Types
Overview

What reference types are

They store pointers to data. Assigning copies the pointer, so multiple references may point to the same storage location.

Arrays
Fixed-size and dynamic. State arrays default to storage; local arrays require memory/storage annotation.
Strings & bytes
Strings are dynamic byte arrays and manipulation is gas-heavy. Use abi.encodePacked for concatenation.
More reference types
Structs
Group fields into a single custom type. Can be storage or memory depending on usage.
Mappings
Key-value lookups that live in storage and are efficient. Note: mappings cannot be iterated directly.
Key Takeaway

Reference types are powerful for complex state but require careful data location choices to avoid unintentional state changes and gas costs.

screens.title: Storage vs. Memory — choosing the right location
screens.subtitle: How storage and memory affect persistence, gas, and behavior

narration.text: Storage and memory are the two primary data locations for reference types in Solidity, and choosing between them determines whether a variable persists and how much gas it costs. Storage is persistent on-chain state — variables declared outside functions are storage by default and any write to storage costs gas and will persist across transactions. Memory exists only for the duration of a function call; it is cheaper and discarded after execution. A common pattern: when you need a temporary copy of a large array for computation or to return to a caller, allocate it in memory. Conversely, when you want to update the contract's long-term state, write to storage. The practical hazard is unintentional storage assignment: declaring a local variable as a storage reference copies the pointer, so mutating it changes the original state. For example, assigning User storage u = users[msg. sender]; will allow mutations to persist. If you intended a local copy, declare User memory u and then modify u without changing storage. The correct selection prevents accidental gas-heavy writes and surprising state changes. As a mental checklist: ask, does this data need to persist? If yes, storage. If not, memory.

keyIdea.title: Data location rule
keyIdea.text: Use storage for persistent state that must survive transactions and memory for temporary, cheaper working copies during function execution.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Storage vs Memory
Process

Decision flow

  1. Do you need persistence across transactions? If yes, use storage.
  2. Is the data temporary for computation or return values? If yes, use memory.
  3. Are you assigning a reference inside a function? Be explicit: storage or memory.
  4. When returning reference types, return a memory copy to the caller.
Concrete example
// storage reference - mutates state
User storage u = users[msg.sender];
u.isActive = false; // changes storage

// memory copy - safe local use
User memory copy = users[msg.sender];
copy.isActive = false; // does not change storage
Key Takeaway

Always specify memory or storage for local reference types and choose based on persistence needs to avoid accidental state writes and extra gas.

screens.title: Arrays — fixed-size vs dynamic
screens.subtitle: Storing collections and manipulating them safely and efficiently

narration.text: Arrays let you store ordered collections of elements of the same type. Fixed-size arrays have a compile-time bound like uint[5], while dynamic arrays can grow and shrink using push and pop. When declared as state variables, dynamic arrays live in storage and push operations change persistent state and cost gas. When you declare an array within a function, you must choose memory or storage. Creating a memory array requires allocating the size at creation, for example new uint[](_count). The chapter shows a common pattern: uint[] public ages as a storage array with an addAge function that pushes a new value. For read-only processing, you may take an input array in memory and return a new memory array after computing results, like doubling values. Be mindful of bounds: accessing an out-of-bounds index will revert the transaction. A common mistake is returning a storage reference; Solidity disallows returning a storage pointer to external callers so you must copy to memory. Key practice: prefer memory for temporary arrays, push to storage only when you truly want to persist additions, and validate indices before access.

keyIdea.title: Arrays
keyIdea.text: Use fixed arrays when size is known at compile time; use dynamic arrays for variable collections and manage storage vs memory explicitly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Arrays
Arrays at a glance

Fixed-size and Dynamic

Fixed-size arrays reserve a compile-time length. Dynamic arrays grow with push and shrink with pop. State arrays default to storage.

State example
uint[] public ages;

function addToArray(uint _value) public {
  ages.push(_value);
}
Memory arrays

Temporary arrays inside functions

You create memory arrays with new and return them to callers as memory copies. This is cheaper than persistent writes and required for safe returns of reference types.

Example
function getRecentAges(uint _count) public view returns (uint[] memory) {
  uint[] memory recent = new uint[](_count);
  // populate recent
  return recent;
}
Key Takeaway

Persist only when needed. Use memory for computation and return copies to callers to avoid exposing storage pointers.

screens.title: Strings and string manipulation
screens.subtitle: Strings are dynamic bytes — cost, encoding, and safe handling

narration.text: Strings in Solidity are dynamic arrays of UTF-8 encoded bytes and behave like reference types. That means operations on strings copy or reference memory depending on the context, and string manipulation can be gas-intensive. Solidity does not provide native high-level concatenation like some higher-level languages; instead, the common pattern for concatenation is using abi. encodePacked and then casting to string, which allocates memory and may be expensive on-chain. Because string operations are often unnecessary in critical paths, prefer off-chain processing when possible or use indexed identifiers and hashes on-chain. Remember that strings are reference types, so passing a string parameter into a function typically uses memory and should be declared string memory to make the lifetime explicit. Also be aware that string length operations traverse bytes and that converting between bytes and string requires attention to encoding. The practical rule is to minimize on-chain string manipulation, use bytes when you need raw binary handling, and treat string concatenation as a potentially costly operation. Strings and string manipulation means strings are dynamic reference types; string operations are gas-expensive. use encoding and hashes to reduce on-chain work.. In practical terms, strings are dynamic bytes — cost, encoding, and safe handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Strings
keyIdea.text: Strings are dynamic reference types; string operations are gas-expensive. Use encoding and hashes to reduce on-chain work.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Strings
Definition

Strings are dynamic bytes

They are reference types and may require memory annotation inside functions. Manipulation tends to be gas-heavy.

Common pattern
Use abi.encodePacked to concatenate and return a memory string when needed, but prefer off-chain processing if possible.
Practical advice
  • Avoid heavy string operations on-chain.
  • Use bytes for lower-level binary handling.
  • Pass strings as memory parameters for temporary use.
Key Takeaway

Minimize string work in critical on-chain paths; favor hashes and off-chain processing for heavy text tasks.

screens.title: Structs and mappings
screens.subtitle: Modeling complex records and efficient lookups

narration.text: Structs and mappings are the building blocks for structured on-chain state. Structs let you bundle related fields into a single type, combining value and reference fields. For example the chapter defines a Product struct that includes id, name, price, and available — this models an entity as a single, coherent unit and can be stored as a state variable or in mappings. Mappings are key-value stores that live in storage and provide efficient lookups by key, such as mapping from address to User or id to product name. A notable limitation: mappings are not iterable, so you cannot enumerate keys on-chain without separately tracking them. When you retrieve a struct from storage inside a function, explicitly choose memory or storage: modifying a storage struct reference will update persistent state, whereas copying into memory lets you make safe temporary changes. Use mappings for fast access patterns, structs for grouped data, and combine them: mappings(address => User) is common. Watch for storage side effects when working with nested reference types and make explicit copies when you want to avoid persisting changes. Structs and mappings means use structs to model complex records and mappings for o(1) lookups. remember: mappings live in storage and aren't iterable.. In practical terms, modeling complex records and efficient lookups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Structs & Mappings
keyIdea.text: Use structs to model complex records and mappings for O(1) lookups. Remember: mappings live in storage and aren't iterable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Structs & Mappings
Structs

Grouped fields for complex data

Use structs to encapsulate related properties. They can be stored in state or used as memory copies inside functions.

Example
struct Product { uint id; string name; uint price; bool available; }
Product public myProduct; // storage
Mappings

Efficient key-value storage

Mappings map a key type to a value type and are stored in contract storage. They provide efficient lookup but are not iterable.

Example
mapping(address => uint) public balances; // persistent balance lookup
Key Takeaway

Combine structs and mappings for organized persistent state, and be explicit about copies to avoid unintended storage mutations.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.subtitle: Overflow, storage misuse, string costs, and payable confusion

narration.text: This lesson collects common pitfalls the chapter highlights and how to avoid them. Integer overflow and underflow were silent before Solidity 0.8.0, but now arithmetic overflows revert by default — a major safety improvement. If you use unchecked blocks you bypass that protection, so only do so with discipline. Second, confusing storage and memory leads to costly mistakes: accidentally declaring a local reference as storage can mutate state and cost a lot of gas. Always explicitly annotate local reference types. Third, string manipulation is expensive on-chain; prefer off-chain text processing or store hashes on-chain and manipulate strings off-chain. Fourth, using address when you intended to transfer Ether is dangerous — use address payable to denote transfer capability. Finally, fixed-size versus dynamic arrays require bounds checks; out-of-bounds access reverts. A helpful practice is to include a quick checklist in your review or tests: check integer ranges, verify storage/memory usage, avoid heavy string operations in hot paths, and confirm address payable where transfers occur. These small checks prevent expensive and hard-to-debug contract bugs. Common mistakes and safety notes means guard against overflow, choose memory vs storage deliberately, minimize string work, and mark payable addresses explicitly.. In practical terms, overflow, storage misuse, string costs, and payable confusion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Guard against overflow, choose memory vs storage deliberately, minimize string work, and mark payable addresses explicitly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Common Mistakes

Safety checklist for common mistakes

Apply these checks during coding and reviews to avoid costly errors.

Overflow / underflow
Since 0.8.0, arithmetic overflows revert; avoid unchecked unless you intend wrap behavior and have tests to match.
Storage vs memory errors
Declare local reference types explicitly. If you need a local independent copy, use memory; if you need to persist changes, use storage.
String costs
Avoid heavy on-chain string manipulation. Store hashes or process text off-chain when feasible.
address vs address payable
Use payable for transfer targets to avoid accidental send failures. The type documents intent and enforces safety.
Pro tip

Add type and location checks to unit tests. Verifying storage vs memory and integer ranges in tests prevents subtle runtime failures.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Core definitions and practical rules of thumb

narration.text: Let's cement the core concepts. Value types store their own data and copy independently, so use them when you need isolated behavior. Reference types store pointers and can lead to shared-state side effects — always be explicit about memory or storage. Use uint for non-negative quantities and choose widths that match your domain to save storage. Mark addresses payable when you plan to send Ether, and treat bytesN as compact fixed-size storage for hashes or identifiers. Arrays can be fixed or dynamic; remember that dynamic state arrays persist and cost gas to modify. Structs and mappings provide structured persistent state and efficient lookups but require careful handling of nested reference types. Finally, make the safety checklist part of your routine: check integer ranges, avoid unnecessary string work on-chain, and be deliberate about storage writes. These principles will reduce bugs and gas costs as you build contracts.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Types and locations affect correctness and cost. Be explicit and choose the simplest type that expresses intent.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Practical short reminders for daily development

narration.text: A quick set of practical reminders closes the chapter. Use uint for non-negative numbers and prefer the smallest width that covers your range to save storage. Declare address payable where you intend to send Ether. Treat strings as potentially expensive and prefer hashes or off-chain processing for heavy text work. When returning arrays from functions, Solidity requires returning a memory copy rather than a storage pointer; specify memory in the return signature. And finally, add quick tests for storage vs memory behavior so your unit tests catch accidental persistent writes. These short rules will keep contracts predictable and reduce expensive mistakes. What to Remember means prefer explicit types and locations, test for state vs temporary behavior, and avoid unnecessary on-chain string work.. In practical terms, practical short reminders for daily development. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Developer Reminders

Quick Reminders

Pick sizes
Use the smallest integer width that fits your data domain.
Mark payable
Use address payable for transfer recipients to make intent explicit.
Test locations
Write unit tests that assert whether changes persist or are local copies.
Final takeaway

Types and data locations are not just syntax; they are essential design choices that affect gas, security, and correctness. Make them explicit and test them.
